pre-processing.label: Pre-processing
pre-processing.description: Problem formulation, data collection, and data preparation — laying the groundwork for responsible AI.

in-processing.label: In-processing
in-processing.description: Model selection, training, evaluation, and fairness analysis — building the model responsibly.

post-processing.label: Post-processing
post-processing.description: Deployment, monitoring, accountability, and user engagement — sustaining responsible AI in production.

areas.name: Techno-solutionist Bias
areas.description: Using complex AI/ML when simpler, cheaper methods would solve the problem just as well.
areas.context: Deep learning on small datasets when basic statistical models would perform comparably. Elaborate ML pipelines where a rule-based system or simple dashboard would meet the actual need.
areas.introduced: Problem formulation — when the team assumes AI is the right approach without comparing alternatives.
areas.exposed: The deployed system fails to outperform simpler methods, or the resource costs outweigh the benefits.
areas.mitigated: Structured alternatives analysis, cost-benefit evaluation, and stakeholder consultation during problem definition.

references.citation: Selbst, A. D., boyd, d., Friedler, S. A., Venkatasubramanian, S., & Vertesi, J. (2019). Fairness and Abstraction in Sociotechnical Systems. FAT* '19.
references.relevance: Identifies the Solutionism Trap — the assumption that technology is the appropriate tool to solve a social problem. Directly names and explains the mechanism of techno-solutionism in AI.

areas.name: Data Scarcity & Availability Bias
areas.description: Training data that is too sparse or not relevant to the problem, producing models that miss real-world patterns.
areas.context: Missing demographic variables during digitization. Underrepresentation of minority or rural populations. Convenience sampling that limits dataset diversity.
areas.introduced: Data collection — the available datasets do not cover the target population.
areas.exposed: Models produce inaccurate predictions for underrepresented populations or scenarios.
areas.mitigated: Data completeness audits, representativeness analysis, and augmentation strategies.

references.citation: Sambasivan, N., et al. (2021). 'Everyone wants to do the model work, not the data work': Data Cascades in High-Stakes AI. CHI '21.
references.relevance: CHI Best Paper. 53 practitioner interviews documenting why data scarcity happens — organizational incentives, resource allocation, prestige bias.

areas.name: Historical & Societal Bias
areas.description: Training data that reflects existing social and historical biases, producing models that perpetuate or amplify those inequities.
areas.context: Legacy records encoding racial or gender biases from past institutional practices. Historical lending data reflecting redlining. Hiring data shaped by decades of unequal access.
areas.introduced: Data drawn from institutions with discriminatory histories (redlining records, biased hiring data, unequal access to services).
areas.exposed: Model predictions systematically disadvantage the same groups that historical practices disadvantaged.
areas.mitigated: Contextual bias analysis, protected group identification, and bias-aware data preprocessing.

references.citation: Buolamwini, J., & Gebru, T. (2018). Gender Shades: Intersectional Accuracy Disparities in Commercial Gender Classification. FAT*.
references.relevance: Empirical audit showing how historical underrepresentation creates measurable accuracy disparities across race and gender.

areas.name: Population Bias
areas.description: The population used during design does not match the population the system will actually serve, leading to unreliable results.
areas.context: Models trained on data from one region deployed to another. Systems built for one demographic group applied to a different one without validation.
areas.introduced: Design phase — the defined target population does not match the actual deployment context.
areas.exposed: Deployed models perform poorly for user groups not represented in training data.
areas.mitigated: Stakeholder mapping, deployment context analysis, and cross-population validation.

references.citation: Obermeyer, Z., Powers, B., Vogeli, C., & Mullainathan, S. (2019). Dissecting Racial Bias in an Algorithm Used to Manage the Health of Populations. Science, 366(6464).
references.relevance: Demonstrates how a healthcare algorithm used cost as a proxy for need, systematically underidentifying Black patients.

areas.name: Sampling & Generalization Bias
areas.description: Non-random or uneven sampling that produces unrepresentative data, causing models to generalize poorly.
areas.context: Oversampling easily accessible sources while undersampling hard-to-reach groups. Non-representative train/test splits across heterogeneous populations.
areas.introduced: Sampling methodology design — how subjects or records are selected for inclusion.
areas.exposed: Model predictions are unreliable for undersampled groups or conditions.
areas.mitigated: Stratified sampling, statistical significance testing across groups, and balanced data collection.

references.citation: Suresh, H., & Guttag, J. (2021). A Framework for Understanding Sources of Harm throughout the Machine Learning Life Cycle. EAAMO '21.
references.relevance: Formalizes sampling bias by distinguishing target, use, and development populations — explains how sampling bias enters the pipeline.

areas.name: Privacy & Consent Violations
areas.description: Collecting, storing, or processing personal data without proper informed consent, legal authorization, or protection measures.
areas.context: Data collected without informed consent. Cross-border data sharing without governance frameworks. Insufficient anonymization of sensitive records.
areas.introduced: Data collection and storage — consent and privacy mechanisms are inadequate or absent.
areas.exposed: Sensitive personal information is leaked, misused, or shared without authorization.
areas.mitigated: Informed consent protocols, data anonymization techniques, access controls, and compliance with national data protection laws.

references.citation: Rocher, L., Hendrickx, J. M., & de Montjoye, Y.-A. (2019). Estimating the success of re-identifications in incomplete datasets. Nature Communications, 10, 3069.
references.relevance: Proves 99.98% of individuals can be re-identified with 15 attributes — fundamentally challenges the anonymize-and-share paradigm.

areas.name: Labeling Bias
areas.description: Inconsistent, inaccurate, or biased labeling of training data that introduces systematic errors.
areas.context: Inconsistent coding across multilingual systems. Subjective labels varying by annotator expertise. Annotation inconsistencies in multi-site data collection.
areas.introduced: The labeling and annotation process — annotator disagreement, unclear guidelines, or insufficient expertise.
areas.exposed: Model predictions reflect labeling inconsistencies rather than true patterns in the data.
areas.mitigated: Inter-rater reliability assessment, clear labeling guidelines, and label auditing.

references.citation: Northcutt, C. G., Athalye, A., & Mueller, J. (2021). Pervasive Label Errors in Test Sets Destabilize Machine Learning Benchmarks. NeurIPS 2021.
references.relevance: Quantified ~6% label error rate across 10 major benchmarks. Proves labeling bias is systemic and destabilizes model selection.

areas.name: Algorithmic Discrimination
areas.description: A model that systematically produces different outcomes for protected groups, resulting in unfair treatment or disparate impact.
areas.context: Prediction models underperforming for minority groups. Differential accuracy across age groups, genders, or income brackets. Screening tools that disproportionately flag one demographic.
areas.introduced: Model training — the algorithm learns biased patterns from data or optimizes for the wrong objective.
areas.exposed: Subgroup performance analysis reveals significant disparities across protected groups.
areas.mitigated: Fairness metrics evaluation, subgroup analysis, and bias mitigation techniques.

references.citation: Hardt, M., Price, E., & Srebro, N. (2016). Equality of Opportunity in Supervised Learning. NeurIPS 2016.
references.relevance: Introduced equalized odds and equality of opportunity as formal fairness constraints with practical post-processing methods.

areas.name: Aggregation Bias
areas.description: Pooling data across diverse groups masks subgroup differences, producing models that work on average but fail for specific populations.
areas.context: Aggregating across geographically or demographically diverse populations hides region-specific patterns. Combining urban and rural data without stratification.
areas.introduced: Data aggregation and model training — heterogeneous populations treated as a single group.
areas.exposed: Overall model performance is acceptable but subgroup performance varies significantly.
areas.mitigated: Disaggregated analysis, stratified model evaluation, and consideration of separate models for distinct populations.

references.citation: Suresh, H., & Guttag, J. (2021). A Framework for Understanding Sources of Harm throughout the Machine Learning Life Cycle. EAAMO '21.
references.relevance: Formally defines aggregation bias as a distinct harm type where pooling heterogeneous data masks subgroup differences.

areas.name: Opacity & Unexplainability
areas.description: Using complex models whose decisions cannot be understood, explained, or audited by the people affected.
areas.context: Black-box models used for high-stakes decisions without explanation mechanisms. Prediction scores that cannot be explained to end-users, regulators, or affected individuals.
areas.introduced: Model selection — complex architectures chosen without explainability considerations.
areas.exposed: End-users, regulators, or affected individuals cannot understand why the model made a specific prediction.
areas.mitigated: Explainability methods (SHAP, LIME, feature importance), model documentation, and selecting interpretable models where appropriate.

references.citation: Rudin, C. (2019). Stop explaining black box machine learning models for high stakes decisions and use interpretable models instead. Nature Machine Intelligence, 1(5).
references.relevance: Challenges the accuracy-interpretability tradeoff myth and argues interpretable models should replace black boxes for high-stakes decisions.

areas.name: Metric Selection Bias
areas.description: Picking evaluation metrics that fail to capture what matters for the actual use case, especially around fairness.
areas.context: Optimizing for accuracy on imbalanced datasets instead of recall. Ignoring false negative rates where missed cases carry severe consequences.
areas.introduced: Evaluation design — performance metrics selected without context analysis.
areas.exposed: Models appear performant by chosen metrics but fail in deployment due to unmeasured dimensions.
areas.mitigated: Contextual metric selection, multi-metric evaluation, and fairness-aware metric frameworks.

references.citation: Kleinberg, J., Mullainathan, S., & Raghavan, M. (2017). Inherent Trade-Offs in the Fair Determination of Risk Scores. ITCS '17.
references.relevance: Mathematical proof that calibration, balance for negatives, and balance for positives cannot be simultaneously satisfied unless base rates are equal.

areas.name: Model Robustness Failure
areas.description: Models that break when real-world data distribution shifts from what they were trained on.
areas.context: A model trained on high-quality controlled data failing on noisy field-collected inputs. Performance degradation on populations with different characteristics than the training set.
areas.introduced: Training — models not stress-tested against realistic deployment conditions.
areas.exposed: Models fail or degrade significantly under real-world conditions that differ from training data.
areas.mitigated: Robustness testing, cross-validation across diverse conditions, and sensitivity analysis.

references.citation: Koh, P. W., Sagawa, S., et al. (2021). WILDS: A Benchmark of in-the-Wild Distribution Shifts. ICML 2021.
references.relevance: 10 curated datasets spanning healthcare, ecology, and NLP for evaluating robustness under real distribution shift.

areas.name: Reproducibility Failure
areas.description: Results that cannot be reproduced because code, data, parameters, or experimental setup were not properly documented.
areas.context: Undocumented hyperparameters. Missing random seeds. Non-versioned code and data pipelines that change silently between runs.
areas.introduced: Model development — documentation and versioning practices are inadequate.
areas.exposed: Other researchers or auditors cannot reproduce the reported results.
areas.mitigated: Code versioning, experiment tracking, documentation standards, and model cards.

references.citation: Kapoor, S., & Narayanan, A. (2023). Leakage and the Reproducibility Crisis in Machine-Learning-Based Science. Patterns, 4(9).
references.relevance: Systemic data leakage across 329 papers in 17 scientific fields. Proves the reproducibility crisis is structural, not anecdotal.

areas.name: Data Integrity Compromise
areas.description: Data corruption, unauthorized modification, or quality degradation during processing.
areas.context: Corrupted records during ETL from legacy to modern systems. Quality issues in cross-institutional data harmonization. Silent encoding errors in automated pipelines.
areas.introduced: Data processing and transformation pipelines — integrity checks are missing or insufficient.
areas.exposed: Model behavior is erratic or produces unexpected results due to data quality issues.
areas.mitigated: Data validation pipelines, integrity checks, access controls, and audit logging.

references.citation: Sculley, D., et al. (2015). Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems. NeurIPS 2015.
references.relevance: Documents pipeline jungles, data dependency issues, and configuration concerns. Explains how data integrity degrades in real ML systems.

areas.name: Deployment Drift
areas.description: Model performance degrades over time as real-world conditions drift from what the training data represented.
areas.context: Changing population characteristics, economic conditions, or user behavior while models remain static. Seasonal or structural shifts in the underlying data distribution.
areas.introduced: Post-deployment — models are not monitored for performance changes over time.
areas.exposed: Model predictions become increasingly inaccurate in production.
areas.mitigated: Continuous monitoring dashboards, scheduled retraining, and drift detection alerts.

references.citation: Lu, J., et al. (2019). Learning under Concept Drift: A Review. IEEE TKDE, 31(12).
references.relevance: Most comprehensive concept drift review covering detection methods, understanding framework, and adaptation strategies.

areas.name: Lack of Human Oversight
areas.description: AI-driven decisions deployed without adequate human review, validation, or override mechanisms.
areas.context: Automated recommendations accepted without expert review. Screening decisions made without a mechanism for human override or correction.
areas.introduced: Deployment design — human oversight mechanisms are not incorporated.
areas.exposed: Harmful automated decisions are made without human intervention or correction.
areas.mitigated: Human-in-the-loop design, domain expert review protocols, and override mechanisms.

references.citation: Parasuraman, R., & Manzey, D. H. (2010). Complacency and Bias in Human Use of Automation. Human Factors, 52(3).
references.relevance: Integrates automation complacency and automation bias via attentional mechanisms — explains why human oversight systematically fails even when required.

areas.name: Accountability Gap
areas.description: No clear ownership, liability, or accountability structure when the AI system produces harmful or incorrect outputs.
areas.context: Unclear responsibility when AI-assisted decisions lead to adverse outcomes. No accountability framework for systems shared across multiple organizations.
areas.introduced: Governance structures fail to assign clear ownership of AI system outcomes.
areas.exposed: Harmful AI decisions occur and no entity is accountable for remediation.
areas.mitigated: Governance frameworks, accountability matrices, incident response plans, and documentation.

references.citation: Raji, I. D., et al. (2020). Closing the AI Accountability Gap: Defining an End-to-End Framework for Internal Algorithmic Auditing. FAT* '20.
references.relevance: Introduced SMACTR framework for end-to-end internal algorithmic auditing. Explains what the accountability gap looks like and provides a framework for closing it.

areas.name: User Literacy Deficit
areas.description: End-users who do not sufficiently understand the system's capabilities, limitations, and appropriate use.
areas.context: Frontline staff unable to interpret confidence scores. End-users misinterpreting AI-flagged alert levels or output categories.
areas.introduced: Deployment plans do not include user training and education.
areas.exposed: End-users misuse, over-rely on, or distrust AI system outputs due to lack of understanding.
areas.mitigated: User training programs, accessible documentation, contextual help systems, and literacy assessments.

references.citation: Long, D., & Magerko, B. (2020). What is AI Literacy? Competencies and Design Considerations. CHI '20.
references.relevance: Definitive AI literacy framework identifying 17 competencies across 5 themes with 16 design considerations.

areas.name: Environmental Impact
areas.description: Significant energy consumption and carbon footprint from training and running AI models.
areas.context: Carbon footprint of training large models in resource-constrained settings. Energy costs of continuous model inference at scale.
areas.introduced: Model architecture and deployment infrastructure decisions ignore environmental considerations.
areas.exposed: Energy consumption and carbon emissions are measured and found disproportionate to benefits.
areas.mitigated: Efficient model architectures, green computing practices, and environmental impact assessments.

references.citation: Strubell, E., Ganesh, A., & McCallum, A. (2019). Energy and Policy Considerations for Deep Learning in NLP. ACL 2019.
references.relevance: First rigorous quantification of AI training energy costs (284 tonnes CO2 for a single NAS run). Catalyzed the Green AI movement.

areas.name: Feedback Loop Absence
areas.description: No mechanism for affected communities, end-users, or stakeholders to provide feedback, contest decisions, or report issues.
areas.context: No avenue for people affected by AI decisions to appeal. No community feedback channel for deployed systems. Issues that persist because no one can report them.
areas.introduced: Deployment design does not incorporate feedback and redress mechanisms.
areas.exposed: System errors persist undetected, or affected individuals have no recourse.
areas.mitigated: Feedback platforms, appeal mechanisms, community engagement, and regular stakeholder consultations.

references.citation: Alfrink, K., et al. (2022). Contestable AI by Design: Towards a Framework. Minds and Machines, 33(4).
references.relevance: Most comprehensive design framework for building contestability into AI systems. Explains what feedback loops should look like and how to design them.

areas.name: Documentation Deficit
areas.description: Missing or incomplete documentation of the AI system: model cards, datasheets, codebooks, and deployment specifications.
areas.context: Missing model cards for deployed models. Absent datasheets for assembled datasets. No codebooks for deployed systems.
areas.introduced: Documentation is not prioritized throughout the development and deployment lifecycle.
areas.exposed: Auditors, regulators, or successors cannot understand or evaluate the system.
areas.mitigated: Documentation templates (model cards, datasheets, codebooks), automated documentation generation, and documentation reviews.

references.citation: Mitchell, M., et al. (2019). Model Cards for Model Reporting. FAT* '19.
references.relevance: Most widely adopted AI documentation standard covering intended use, performance metrics, limitations, and ethical considerations.

controls.name: Stratified Model Evaluation
controls.description: Sometimes one model cannot serve everyone well. Check whether separate models or stratified approaches would be fairer.
